schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter

Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

<system-reminder>

content.content:
# Evaluation-game estimands and incentive-response testbed

## Scope

This is a small exact, finite synthetic testbed. It does not call a model,
collect transcripts, simulate interacting agents, or identify strategic intent.
It builds on the separation among game, case distribution, measurement, and
claim in [evaluation_design_calculus.md](evaluation_design_calculus.md). It
does not alter the frozen v3 sandbagging results or protocol.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_testbed.py --output output/evaluation_game_testbed.json
python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_testbed.py -q
```

The output is exact synthetic fixture evidence, not model or agent evidence.
It stores rational values as strings and will not overwrite an existing output.

## Four non-interchangeable estimands

Fix \(\mathcal E=\langle G,\Pi,D,Z,J,\mathcal A,C\rangle\). A score alone
does not say which object changed.

| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline gain | \(B=V_{\pi_1}(d)-V_{\pi_0}(d)\) with a named case law and judgment | Robustness or strategic stability |
| Robust regret | \(R(\pi;\mathcal Q)=\max_{q\in\mathcal Q}[\max_{\pi'}V_{\pi'}(q)-V_\pi(q)]\) | A baseline gain or a measurement gap |
| Discrimination gap | \(\mathrm{TV}(Z_\#P_{\pi_1},Z_\#P_{\pi_0})\) | Utility, regret, or player information |
| Exploitability | \(\max_i[\sup_{\pi_i'}\mathbb EU_i(\pi_i',\pi_{-i})-\mathbb EU_i(\pi)]\) | Generalization or welfare |

The finite fixtures make baseline gain and robust regret both one half. Their
matching numbers are intentional: their source objects and interpretation remain
different, so they must not be combined or relabeled as each other.
Both policies in the corrected baseline fixture receive the revealed state:
the baseline always chooses left and the candidate follows the observation.
The game and case law are consequently fixed for that comparison.

## Observation-only Hide versus player-facing hiding

Observation-only `Hide` belongs to acquisition. After players act, apply a
common Markov kernel \(H(z'\mid z)\) to each completed record:

\[
P_H(z'\mid\pi)=\sum_z H(z'\mid z)P(z\mid\pi).
\]

It does not change legal actions, player histories, transitions, or payoffs.
In the fixture, perfectly correct and perfectly wrong traces have visible
total-variation discrimination gap one. The common kernel maps both to
`redacted`, leaving an acquired-record gap of zero and demonstrating finite
data processing: \(\mathrm{TV}(H_\#P,H_\#Q)\leq\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)\).

Removing information from a player before action instead changes \(O_i\) in
\(G\). In the two-location game, the optimal value falls from one to one half.
That is a game intervention, not offline measurement redaction. An adapter that
removes player feedback must type it that way irrespective of its method name.

## Strategic checks, costs, and falsifiers

The social-dilemma fixture enumerates a pure equilibrium set and reports the
selected outcome under `enumerate_pure_nash_then_lexicographically_select`; it
does not present the outcome as controller behavior. At `share, share`, exact
exploitability is two. Searching only the `share` deviation returns zero, which
is marked as a lower bound rather than exploitability. A matching-pennies
fixture separately checks equal primal maximin and dual minimax witnesses at
zero. It is not a generic equilibrium solver.

Falsifiers for an applied strategic interpretation are an illegal deviation
class, private state leaked to the search, an unspecified adaptation or
equilibrium-selection rule, dependent payoff estimates, or calling a restricted
search exact exploitability. Report the restriction and withhold that stronger
claim when any appears.

## Incentive-response design for sandbagging investigation

The estimand is a behavioral incentive-response contrast, not intent. Let
\(Y_{c,d,g}\) be a blinded score with condition \(c\), difficulty \(d\), and
grader-severity stratum \(g\):

\[
Y=\mu+\alpha_c+\beta_d+\gamma_g+\eta_{c,d}+\varepsilon.
\]

Match paired control/incentive tasks within \((d,g)\), estimate
\(\tau_d=\mathbb E[Y_{0,d,g}-Y_{1,d,g}]\), and reserve untouched blocks to
test \(\iota=\tau_{hard}-\tau_{easy}\). Pairing cancels additive difficulty
and grader severity; it does not establish prompt equivalence or intent.
Selection of strata, allocation, and any target family remains in training data;
the interaction is tested only in the held-out confirmation data.

For acquisition, condition 0 gives the ordinary task and performance objective;
condition 1 adds a preregistered evaluation-contingent incentive frame while
holding task instructions, tools, time budget, scoring rubric, and stated role
fixed. The frame is shown to the participant before acting, so it is a
presentation/incentive intervention on the game, not observation-only Hide.
Use held-out isomorphic task forms matched by difficulty calibrated on separate
data; randomize form-to-condition and AB/BA order in reset contexts. A negative
control uses comparably sized neutral framing with no changed incentive. This
design checks sensitivity to the chosen frame, not compliance with an assumed
internal utility function. Semantic equivalence must be reviewed independently.

Estimate grader severity on independent anchor responses with condition labels
removed. Cross each grader/severity stratum with both conditions and both
difficulties using the same rubric and version; do not assign strict graders
only to the incentive arm. Save response, form, block, assignment, scorer, and
calibration identifiers. Difficulty- or condition-dependent grading errors
require an expanded nuisance model and separate checks. The executable fixture
encodes known additive severity, not estimated severity or verified blinding.

The fixture has four equal-weight equal-variance strata and a 96-score budget.
Each matched pair costs two scored responses. It enumerates the 48-pair integer
allocation minimizing \(\sum_h(1/4)^2/n_h\) and obtains 12 pairs per stratum.
This optimization is conditional on its equal-variance and equal-cost premise.
In an applied study, preregister variance/cost estimates, retain minimum stratum
coverage, and use the resulting Neyman-style allocation without holdout tuning.

The fixture deliberately has no latent intent variable and records
`intent_identified: false`. A contrast can arise from strategic response, benign
role constraints, task changes, condition-dependent scoring, or distribution
shift. Falsifiers include an interaction in negative-incentive controls, failed
prompt-equivalence review, unblinded scoring, grader severity not linked within
pairs, or a selection/holdout block overlap. Any falsifier defeats the strategic
interpretation; it is not evidence of a zero effect.

## Executable confirmation and adversarial checks

`evaluation_game_confirmation.py` now enforces the split on actual synthetic
pair and block records. Every block contains all four difficulty/grader strata.
Duplicate pairs, missing strata, mixed block metadata, reused training IDs,
and confirmation of a different family all raise errors. The selected family
is chosen by training mean gap with lexical ties, before confirmation rows are
generated. Identifiers can detect recorded overlap; they cannot independently
certify independence or prevent an operator from relabeling reused observations.

The saved fixture has two families with eight training blocks each (64 pairs,
128 score operations), then 12 target and 12 negative-control blocks for the
selected family (96 pairs, 192 score operations). The total is **320**. These
are constructed score values, not paid model calls or independent model trials.
The older four-cell arithmetic illustration records eight score values and a
separate *planned* 96-score target allocation; that plan is not an acquisition
receipt. Calibration, prompt review, and scorer qualification costs remain
outside this synthetic count and must be budgeted for an observed study.

Each confirmation block produces an equal-weight incentive-response contrast
and a hard-minus-easy interaction. Two exact two-sided sign tests receive
alpha/2 each, with ties discarded. These test directional consistency under
independent blocks and equiprobable nonzero signs under the null; they do not
test the population mean. The fixture reports the arithmetic means separately.
Its interaction is 1/5, with sign p-value 1/2048 across 12 positive blocks.
This deterministic positive fixture does not measure statistical coverage or
false-positive rates. Training-only effects return a holdout p-value of one.
This budget covers one selected-family evaluation. Multiple subjects or added
confirmatory contrasts require a frozen campaign correction; do not reuse the
same alpha independently for each subject or retune on confirmation outcomes.

Negative controls must have exactly zero paired differences for this fixture's
support flag. This is an arithmetic diagnostic, not an empirical equivalence
test; observed controls would need uncertainty, tolerance margins, adequate
sample sizes, and a preregistered inference procedure. A control bias withholds
the support flag. Passing that flag still leaves `intent_identified: false`.

The allocation optimizer solves the finite integer problem with supplied
weights, paired-difference variances, pair costs, budget, and minimum stratum
counts. Independent exhaustive enumeration checks it with unequal costs and
variances. Its variance objective assumes independent strata. Covariances of
contrasts measured in common blocks require a different objective; the block
confirmation fixture is not claimed to attain that independent-stratum bound.

Additional checks cover 625 rational binary distribution/channel combinations
for total-variation contraction, malformed kernel rejection, and a falsifier
where different policy-specific channels manufacture discrimination. A general
finite matrix certificate reports primal and dual bounds and refuses to certify
an inferior matching-pennies strategy. A coordination-game example reports its
complete Nash set (two pure profiles and one uniformly mixed profile) alongside
two explicit update paths: simultaneous best responses cycle from (0,1), while
row-then-column updates reach (1,1). The former equilibrium enumeration rule is
a selection convention; these new paths supply actual finite adaptation rules.

The verifier's schema 1.1 includes confirmation, allocation, adaptation, and
primal/dual results and source hashes. Run the expanded regressions with:

```powershell
python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_testbed.py tests/test_evaluation_game_confirmation.py -q
```

# Feedback channel: suggested insertions for the evaluation design calculus

Draft 0.2 — 2026-10-12. Suggestions only. Draft 0.2 states the ceiling law for
failure-targeted patching as well as for patching chosen at random.

This file changes nothing in `evaluation_design_calculus.md` or
`evaluation_game_testbed.md`. Each block names a location in those documents,
offers text for it, and states what supports the text. Where a block is adopted,
its wording should be made the author's own. Where it is not, the executable
fixtures still stand by themselves.

The gap being addressed: the calculus already says that a judgment "shown during
play or used for learning ... also enters observations or controller updates"
(§2), and that frozen-controller sensitivity differs from sensitivity "after
retraining, selecting another controller" (§7). It has no operator for that
channel, no estimand for what the channel does to a score, and no record of how
often it was used. A self-improvement loop is that channel applied once per
generation.

## Evidence behind the suggestions

| Level | Source | What it supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Finite verified example | `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_feedback.py`, 30 tests, receipt under `output/evaluation_game_feedback/` | Access-class ordering, one-generation selection gap, noise-ceiling threshold, failed-item enrichment, ledger enforcement |
| Synthetic mechanism result | `output/eval_reuse_toys/` (two seeded simulations, predictions hashed before each run) | Multi-generation behaviour of the gap under score-only and item-level feedback |
| Not available | — | Any language-model loop, any observed controller |

The simulations are JavaScript, seeded, and not exact. Their prediction record
is 5 of 6 in the first run and 3 of 6 in the second, and both overpredicted the
size of the gap. One arm of the second run was added after its sealed results
were seen and is marked exploratory in its own files.

## A. §2, after "Maintain three distinctions"

Suggested fourth distinction:

> 4. A judgment that reaches whatever produces the next controller is a channel.
> Its source set, its access class, and the number of times it was used belong
> in the experiment record. A score measured on a set that fed this channel is a
> selection score. A capability claim needs a set that did not.

## B. §3, operator table

Suggested row:

| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
|---|---|---|
| \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\) | Controller roster/protocol of a later generation | Source set \(s\); access class \(q\in\{\text{sealed},\text{score-only},\text{item-level}\}\); whether the consumer selects among candidates or supplies a training input; generation scope. |

Suggested sentence beneath the table:

> Feedback is not \(\operatorname{Rescore}\), which is offline, and not
> \(\operatorname{Observe}\), which changes what the evaluator records. It reads
> \(J\) restricted to \(s\) and writes \(\Pi\) for the next generation. Declaring
> a set sealed while a score from it reaches the loop is ill-typed.

## C. §4, after the sentence on `Repeat` and reset/carry maps

> Generations joined by Feedback are not independent blocks. The carry map
> carries the controller, and with it whatever of \(s\) the channel transmitted.
> Aggregating a per-generation score across such generations as if each were a
> fresh draw of the same experiment mistakes the unit.

## D. §5, three laws and one observation

**Coarsening law.**

> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
> feedback and not at all by a score.

Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.

**Selection law.**

> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.

Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
listed cells and no limit.

Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.

**Ceiling law.**

> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) in expectation on
> observed labels. Let \(v\) be the controller's observed accuracy before any
> item of \(s\) is memorized. If it memorizes a share \(m/n\) of \(s\) chosen
> without regard to its outcomes, it scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\) and
> crosses the ceiling only when \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). If it memorizes
> items it failed, which is what item-level feedback supplies, it scores
> \(v+m/n\) and crosses when \(m/n>1-\varepsilon-v\): the same threshold
> \((1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\), now as a share of the failed items. Below the
> threshold a ceiling check is silent.

Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold` and
`targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\). Memorizing at random, the
check is silent below \(\tfrac8{13}\) of the set. Patching failures, it is
silent below \(\tfrac4{25}\) of the set, which is \(\tfrac8{13}\) of the failed
items. Both formulas assume a memorized item has no effect on any other item.
The nearest-neighbour learner in the second simulation did not satisfy that,
and it also did not reliably absorb a patch: at \(n=4000\) it patched a quarter
of the set and its reported score stayed at 0.759, below the 0.90 ceiling.

**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**

> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:
> \(\Pr[\text{flipped}\mid\text{failed}]=\varepsilon a/(\varepsilon a+(1-\varepsilon)(1-a))\),
> which exceeds \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(a>\tfrac12\). Feeding failures
> back concentrates label noise in what the next controller is built from.

Support: `failed_item_noise_share`; \(\tfrac4{13}\) against a base rate of
\(\tfrac1{10}\) in the fixture. In the second simulation the measured share
among patched items was 20–29% against the same 10% base rate. This is the
reason the unchecked answer in the Proposer–Solver recipe (atlas §11) matters
once its output is fed back.

Suggested closing sentence, matching the section's existing last line:

> No unconditional claim is made that feedback lowers readout performance. In
> the simulations, score-only selection of fresh training batches raised it.

## E. §7, after the definition of the order effect

> For a controller \(\pi_g\) produced with feedback from \(s\), and a sealed set
> \(r\) from the same sampling law, define the readout gap
> \(\rho_g=V^{s}_{\pi_g}-V^{r}_{\pi_g}\). It compares two measurements of one
> controller, not two designs, so it is not a design difference. A gain series
> computed on \(s\) estimates the change in value plus the change in \(\rho\).

## F. §11, the evaluation card

Suggested amendment to item 6:

> ... and whether any score feeds back into play *or into the production of a
> later controller*.

Suggested additional item:

> 10. **Feedback ledger:** for each evaluation set, its role (selection or
> readout), declared access class, score queries, items fed back, number and
> generation of readouts, and the rule that retires it.

## G. `evaluation_game_testbed.md`, estimand table

Suggested fifth row:

| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
|---|---|---|
| Readout gap | \(\rho=V^{s}_\pi-V^{r}_\pi\), with \(s\) having fed judgment to the loop and \(r\) sealed | A baseline gain, or evidence that capability changed |

Suggested section, placed after "Executable confirmation and adversarial
checks":

> ### Feedback channel and multi-generation ledger
>
> `evaluation_game_feedback.py` extends the single split enforced by `confirm()`
> to a sequence of generations. Sets are declared with a role and an access
> class. Events record a score reaching the loop, items reaching the loop, or an
> experimenter reading a sealed set. Malformed declarations raise, including a
> readout set not declared sealed and identifiers shared across sets. Breaches
> of a well-formed declaration are recorded instead, and move the readout
> endpoint to `not_evaluated`: a breach is a finding about the run. Reads of the
> sealed set are budgeted, since a stop-or-continue decision taken on a readout
> is itself adaptive. Identifiers detect recorded overlap. They do not certify
> independence.
>
> ```powershell
> $env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
> python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_feedback.py --output output/evaluation_game_feedback/feedback_v0_2.json
> python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_feedback.py -q
> ```

## H. What is not delivered

- `Feedback` is not implemented against `hive_lab` adapters or any external
  policy. The module checks declarations and arithmetic.
- No loop with a language model has been run. The first observed-controller
  study would pair a small model with a declared selection set and a sealed
  readout, and report the ledger.
- Partial leakage, where the loop learns failure categories and not items, has
  no fixture.
- The simulations fix one parameter set each. No sweep over candidate count,
  decay rate, or label-noise rate was run.

content.content:
"""Exact, synthetic checks for judgment-to-controller feedback.

Nothing in this module calls a model, trains a learner, or runs an improvement
loop.  It types the channel by which a judgment reaches the process that
produces the next controller, and keeps the resulting *readout gap* separate
from baseline gain, robust regret, discrimination gap, and exploitability.

Three access classes order that channel.  ``sealed`` returns nothing,
``score_only`` returns an aggregate count, ``item_level`` returns per-item
outcomes.  Each is a deterministic coarsening of the next, so the finite
data-processing inequality used for observation-only Hide applies to what the
loop can learn about its own failures.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction as Q
from itertools import product
from math import comb

from spiral_ln.evaluation_game_testbed import _pushforward, _tv

ACCESS_CLASSES = ("sealed", "score_only", "item_level")
ROLES = ("selection", "readout")
EVENT_KINDS = ("score_query", "item_feedback", "readout")


def access_kernel(access: str, items: int) -> dict[str, dict[str, Q]]:
    """Deterministic feedback kernel from per-item outcome records.

    A record is a string of ``0``/``1`` of length ``items``.  The kernel says
    what reaches the loop, not what the evaluator stores.
    """

    if access not in ACCESS_CLASSES:
        raise ValueError("unknown access class")
    if type(items) is not int or items < 1:
        raise ValueError("items must be a positive integer")
    kernel = {}
    for bits in product("01", repeat=items):
        record = "".join(bits)
        if access == "sealed":
            image = "sealed"
        elif access == "score_only":
            image = f"score={record.count('1')}"
        else:
            image = record
        kernel[record] = {image: Q(1)}
    return kernel


def access_order_fixture() -> dict[str, object]:
    """Two controllers with equal scores and different failures.

    Item-level feedback separates them completely; score-only feedback cannot
    separate them at all.  A second pair with different scores is separated by
    both, and no pair is separated through a sealed set.
    """

    same_score = ({"10": Q(1)}, {"01": Q(1)})
    different_score = ({"11": Q(1)}, {"00": Q(1)})
    gaps = {}
    for name, (left, right) in (("same_score", same_score),
                                ("different_score", different_score)):
        gaps[name] = {
            access: _tv(_pushforward(left, access_kernel(access, 2)),
                        _pushforward(right, access_kernel(access, 2)))
            for access in ACCESS_CLASSES
        }
    ordered = all(g["sealed"] <= g["score_only"] <= g["item_level"] for g in gaps.values())
    return {"operator_type": "judgment_to_controller_feedback_kernel",
            "gaps": gaps, "access_classes_ordered_by_coarsening": ordered,
            "acts_between_generations": True, "changes_recorded_evidence": False}


def _binomial_pmf(n: int, p: Q) -> list[Q]:
    return [Q(comb(n, j)) * p**j * (1 - p)**(n - j) for j in range(n + 1)]


def selection_inflation(items: int, candidates: int, p: Q) -> dict[str, Q]:
    """Exact one-generation over-report from keeping the best-scoring candidate.

    Every candidate has the same true success probability ``p`` on each of
    ``items`` independent selection items, and candidates are independent.  The
    reported value is the selected candidate's score on those same items; the
    readout value is its expected score on untouched items, which is ``p``.
    This isolates the selection term.  It says nothing about real gains,
    persistence across generations, or correlated candidates.
    """

    if type(items) is not int or type(candidates) is not int or items < 1 or candidates < 1:
        raise ValueError("items and candidates must be positive integers")
    if not 0 <= p <= 1:
        raise ValueError("p must be a probability")
    pmf = _binomial_pmf(items, p)
    cumulative, running = [], Q(0)
    for mass in pmf:
        running += mass
        cumulative.append(running)
    expected_max = sum(
        j * (cumulative[j]**candidates - (cumulative[j - 1]**candidates if j else Q(0)))
        for j in range(items + 1)
    )
    reported = expected_max / items
    return {"expected_reported": reported, "readout_value": p,
            "readout_gap": reported - p}


def observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Accuracy against observed labels when labels flip independently."""

    if not 0 <= clean_accuracy <= 1 or not 0 <= flip <= 1:
        raise ValueError("probabilities required")
    return clean_accuracy * (1 - flip) + (1 - clean_accuracy) * flip


def noise_ceiling(flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Best observed-label accuracy available to a predictor that cannot see
    which labels flipped."""

    if not 0 <= flip <= 1:
        raise ValueError("flip must be a probability")
    return max(flip, 1 - flip)


def memorized_selection_score(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q, patch_share: Q) -> Q:
    """Selection-set score after memorizing a share of its observed labels.

    The memorized items are chosen independently of whether the controller
    already got them right, so the remainder keep the base observed accuracy.
    Memorized items score one.  Collateral effects of a patch on other items
    are assumed absent, which a real learner need not satisfy.
    """

    if not 0 <= patch_share <= 1:
        raise ValueError("patch share must lie in [0, 1]")
    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    return patch_share + (1 - patch_share) * base


def targeted_patch_selection_score(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q, patch_share: Q) -> Q:
    """Selection-set score after memorizing failed items only.

    This is what item-level feedback supplies: each patch turns one failed
    item into a pass and leaves every other item unchanged.  ``patch_share``
    is measured against the whole set and cannot exceed the failure share.
    """

    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    if not 0 <= patch_share <= 1 - base:
        raise ValueError("patch share must lie between zero and the failure share")
    return base + patch_share


def ceiling_detection_threshold(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Share of the set, memorized independently of outcomes, above which the
    selection score exceeds the noise ceiling.

    Below this share the ceiling check is silent however much was memorized.
    """

    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    if base >= 1:
        raise ValueError("base observed accuracy must be below one")
    return max(Q(0), (noise_ceiling(flip) - base) / (1 - base))


def targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Share of the set, patched on failed items only, above which the
    selection score exceeds the noise ceiling.

    As a share of the failed items this equals ``ceiling_detection_threshold``;
    as a share of the set it is smaller by the failure share.
    """

    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    if base >= 1:
        raise ValueError("base observed accuracy must be below one")
    return max(Q(0), noise_ceiling(flip) - base)


def failed_item_noise_share(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Probability that an item the base predictor fails has a flipped label.

    The predictor errs on the clean label independently of the flip.  It fails
    the observed label either by being right about a flipped item or wrong
    about an unflipped one.
    """

    wrong_because_flipped = flip * clean_accuracy
    wrong_unflipped = (1 - flip) * (1 - clean_accuracy)
    if wrong_because_flipped + wrong_unflipped == 0:
        raise ValueError("the predictor never fails an observed label")
    return wrong_because_flipped / (wrong_because_flipped + wrong_unflipped)


def noise_ceiling_fixture() -> dict[str, Q]:
    clean, flip = Q(4, 5), Q(1, 10)
    base = observed_accuracy(clean, flip)
    targeted = targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold(clean, flip)
    return {
        "clean_accuracy": clean, "flip_probability": flip,
        "base_observed_accuracy": base,
        "noise_ceiling": noise_ceiling(flip),
        "score_half_memorized": memorized_selection_score(clean, flip, Q(1, 2)),
        "score_fully_memorized": memorized_selection_score(clean, flip, Q(1)),
        "ceiling_detection_threshold": ceiling_detection_threshold(clean, flip),
        "targeted_threshold_share_of_set": targeted,
        "targeted_threshold_share_of_failures": targeted / (1 - base),
        "score_all_failures_patched": targeted_patch_selection_score(clean, flip, 1 - base),
        "failed_item_noise_share": failed_item_noise_share(clean, flip),
    }


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvalSet:
    set_id: str
    role: str
    access: str
    item_ids: tuple[str, ...]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LoopEvent:
    generation: int
    set_id: str
    kind: str
    item_ids: tuple[str, ...] = ()


def audit_ledger(sets, events, readout_budget, exhaustion_bound):
    """Check a multi-generation feedback ledger against its declarations.

    Malformed declarations raise.  Breaches of a well-formed declaration are
    recorded, and move the affected endpoint to ``not_evaluated``, because a
    breach is a finding about the run and should survive into its report.

    A ``score_query`` or ``item_feedback`` event means the result reached the
    loop.  A ``readout`` event means the experimenter read a sealed set; if a
    loop-affecting decision followed, that reading is itself adaptive, so the
    number of readouts is budgeted.  Identifiers detect recorded overlap only.
    They cannot certify that two differently named items are independent.
    """

    if not sets:
        raise ValueError("at least one evaluation set must be declared")
    if type(readout_budget) is not int or readout_budget < 1:
        raise ValueError("readout budget must be a positive integer")
    if not exhaustion_bound > 0:
        raise ValueError("exhaustion bound must be positive")
    declared, owner = {}, {}
    for item in sets:
        if (not item.set_id or item.role not in ROLES or item.access not in ACCESS_CLASSES
                or not item.item_ids or len(set(item.item_ids)) != len(item.item_ids)):
            raise ValueError("invalid evaluation set declaration")
        if item.set_id in declared:
            raise ValueError("duplicate set identifier")
        if item.role == "readout" and item.access != "sealed":
            raise ValueError("a readout set must be declared sealed")
        for identifier in item.item_ids:
            if identifier in owner:
                raise ValueError("selection/readout identifiers overlap")
            owner[identifier] = item.set_id
        declared[item.set_id] = item
    if not any(item.role == "readout" for item in sets):
        raise ValueError("no readout set declared")

    state = {
        set_id: {"role": item.role, "declared_access": item.access,
                 "size": len(item.item_ids), "score_queries": 0, "patches": 0,
                 "distinct_patched": set(), "readouts": [], "retired_at": None,
                 "breaches": []}
        for set_id, item in declared.items()
    }
    previous = None
    for event in events:
        if (type(event.generation) is not int or event.generation < 0
                or event.kind not in EVENT_KINDS or event.set_id not in declared):
            raise ValueError("invalid loop event")
        if previous is not None and event.generation < previous:
            raise ValueError("events must be ordered by generation")
        previous = event.generation
        target, record = declared[event.set_id], state[event.set_id]
        if event.kind == "readout":
            if target.role != "readout":
                raise ValueError("readout events apply to readout sets only")
            record["readouts"].append(event.generation)
            if len(record["readouts"]) > readout_budget:
                record["breaches"].append(f"readout budget exceeded at generation {event.generation}")
            continue
        if event.kind == "item_feedback":
            if not event.item_ids or not set(event.item_ids) <= set(target.item_ids):
                raise ValueError("item feedback must name items of its own set")
        if target.role == "readout":
            record["breaches"].append(
                f"{event.kind} exposed the readout set at generation {event.generation}")
            continue
        if record["retired_at"] is not None:
            record["breaches"].append(f"used after retirement at generation {event.generation}")
        allowed = ACCESS_CLASSES.index(target.access)
        needed = ACCESS_CLASSES.index("item_level" if event.kind == "item_feedback" else "score_only")
        if needed > allowed:
            record["breaches"].append(
                f"{event.kind} exceeds declared {target.access} access at generation {event.generation}")
        if event.kind == "score_query":
            record["score_queries"] += 1
        else:
            record["patches"] += len(event.item_ids)
            record["distinct_patched"].update(event.item_ids)
            if (record["retired_at"] is None
                    and Q(record["patches"], record["size"]) > exhaustion_bound):
                record["retired_at"] = event.generation

    report = {"selection": {}, "readout": {},
              "identifier_scope": "recorded overlap only; independence is not certified"}
    for set_id, record in state.items():
        if record["role"] == "selection":
            report["selection"][set_id] = {
                "declared_access": record["declared_access"], "size": record["size"],
                "score_queries": record["score_queries"], "patches": record["patches"],
                "distinct_patched": len(record["distinct_patched"]),
                "patch_share": Q(record["patches"], record["size"]),
                "retired_at_generation": record["retired_at"],
                "breaches": tuple(record["breaches"]),
                "selection_scores_usable_as_endpoints": False,
            }
        else:
            report["readout"][set_id] = {
                "size": record["size"], "readouts": len(record["readouts"]),
                "readout_generations": tuple(record["readouts"]),
                "breaches": tuple(record["breaches"]),
                "endpoint_status": "not_evaluated" if record["breaches"] else "evaluable",
            }
    report["declarations_respected"] = not any(
        entry["breaches"] for group in ("selection", "readout")
        for entry in report[group].values())
    return report


def divergence_flags(points, margin):
    """Compare selection-set and readout-set gains between permitted readouts.

    ``points`` are ``(generation, selection_score, readout_score)`` at strictly
    increasing generations.  A flag voids claims resting on the selection set.
    It does not void the sealed readout.
    """

    points = list(points)
    if len(points) < 2:
        raise ValueError("at least two readout points required")
    if not margin >= 0:
        raise ValueError("margin must be nonnegative")
    rows = []
    for (g0, s0, r0), (g1, s1, r1) in zip(points, points[1:]):
        if type(g0) is not int or type(g1) is not int or g1 <= g0:
            raise ValueError("generations must be strictly increasing integers")
        if not all(0 <= value <= 1 for value in (s0, r0, s1, r1)):
            raise ValueError("scores must lie in [0, 1]")
        divergence = (s1 - s0) - (r1 - r0)
        rows.append({"from_generation": g0, "to_generation": g1,
                     "selection_gain": s1 - s0, "readout_gain": r1 - r0,
                     "divergence": divergence, "readout_gap_at_end": s1 - r1,
                     "flagged": divergence > margin})
    return rows


def run_ledger_fixture() -> dict[str, object]:
    """One respected ledger and one breached ledger over the same declarations."""

    selection = EvalSet("S", "selection", "score_only", tuple(f"s{i}" for i in range(8)))
    readout = EvalSet("R", "readout", "sealed", tuple(f"r{i}" for i in range(8)))
    clean_events = (
        LoopEvent(0, "R", "readout"),
        LoopEvent(1, "S", "score_query"), LoopEvent(1, "S", "score_query"),
        LoopEvent(2, "S", "score_query"), LoopEvent(2, "R", "readout"),
    )
    breached_events = clean_events + (
        LoopEvent(3, "S", "item_feedback", ("s0", "s1")),
        LoopEvent(4, "R", "score_query"),
    )
    return {"respected": audit_ledger((selection, readout), clean_events, 3, Q(1, 2)),
            "breached": audit_ledger((selection, readout), breached_events, 3, Q(1, 2))}


def verify() -> dict[str, object]:
    """Run all exact fixtures and return machine-readable checks."""

    order = access_order_fixture()
    smallest = selection_inflation(1, 2, Q(1, 2))
    ladder = {n: selection_inflation(n, 2, Q(1, 2))["readout_gap"] for n in (1, 4, 16, 64)}
    widening = {k: selection_inflation(4, k, Q(1, 2))["readout_gap"] for k in (1, 2, 4, 16)}
    noise = noise_ceiling_fixture()
    ledgers = run_ledger_fixture()
    flags = divergence_flags(((0, Q(7, 10), Q(7, 10)), (50, Q(4, 5), Q(37, 50)),
                              (100, Q(83, 100), Q(73, 100))), Q(1, 50))
    checks = {
        "item_level_separates_equal_scores_and_score_only_does_not":
            order["gaps"]["same_score"] == {"sealed": Q(0), "score_only": Q(0), "item_level": Q(1)},
        "access_classes_ordered": order["access_classes_ordered_by_coarsening"],
        "two_candidates_one_item_gap_is_quarter": smallest["readout_gap"] == Q(1, 4),
        "single_candidate_has_no_selection_gap": widening[1] == 0,
        "selection_gap_shrinks_with_items": ladder[1] > ladder[4] > ladder[16] > ladder[64] > 0,
        "selection_gap_grows_with_candidates": widening[1] < widening[2] < widening[4] < widening[16],
        "full_memorization_exceeds_noise_ceiling":
            noise["score_fully_memorized"] == 1 > noise["noise_ceiling"],
        "half_memorization_stays_below_ceiling":
            noise["score_half_memorized"] < noise["noise_ceiling"],
        "ceiling_check_threshold_is_eight_thirteenths":
            noise["ceiling_detection_threshold"] == Q(8, 13),
        "targeted_patching_crosses_at_four_twentyfifths_of_set":
            noise["targeted_threshold_share_of_set"] == Q(4, 25)
            and noise["targeted_threshold_share_of_failures"] == noise["ceiling_detection_threshold"],
        "failed_items_enriched_for_flipped_labels":
            noise["failed_item_noise_share"] == Q(4, 13) > noise["flip_probability"],
        "respected_ledger_leaves_readout_evaluable":
            ledgers["respected"]["declarations_respected"]
            and ledgers["respected"]["readout"]["R"]["endpoint_status"] == "evaluable",
        "breached_ledger_withholds_endpoint":
            ledgers["breached"]["readout"]["R"]["endpoint_status"] == "not_evaluated"
            and bool(ledgers["breached"]["selection"]["S"]["breaches"]),
        "selection_scores_never_endpoints":
            not ledgers["respected"]["selection"]["S"]["selection_scores_usable_as_endpoints"],
        "divergence_flags_fire_when_selection_outruns_readout":
            [row["flagged"] for row in flags] == [True, True]
            and flags[1]["readout_gain"] < 0 < flags[1]["selection_gain"],
    }
    return {"evidence_status": "exact_synthetic_fixtures_not_model_or_agent_evidence",
            "checks": checks, "all_passed": all(checks.values()),
            "access_order": order,
            "selection_inflation": {"one_item_two_candidates": smallest,
                                    "gap_by_items_two_candidates": ladder,
                                    "gap_by_candidates_four_items": widening},
            "noise_ceiling": noise, "ledger": ledgers, "divergence": flags}

# Eval exhaustion toy: predictions frozen before first run

Written 2026-10-11, before `sim.js` was executed. Hash of this file and of
`sim.js` is recorded in `SEAL.txt` before the run.

## Question

When a self-improvement loop selects candidates on a reused held-out set
(score-only feedback), how far does the reported score separate from
population accuracy, and how does that distort a takeoff readout?

## Model (all parameters fixed here)

- Items: difficulty b ~ N(0, 1.5^2). Model-item quirk u ~ N(0, 1).
- A model solves item i iff a - b_i + u_i > 0 (deterministic evaluation).
- Population accuracy is closed form: Phi(a / sqrt(1.5^2 + 1)).
- Start: a0 chosen so population accuracy = 0.26.
- Each generation g = 1..100, K = 16 candidates. Candidate = incumbent plus
  - general change da = s_g * z, s_g = 0.06 * 0.95^(g-1)  (true gain ratio 0.95)
  - quirk re-roll u' = cos(phi) u + sin(phi) z, sin(phi) = 0.2
- Arms
  - FRESH: candidates and incumbent scored on a new block of n items each
    generation; accept best candidate if it beats the incumbent on that block.
  - REUSE-NAIVE: one fixed set of n items; accept best candidate if its score
    exceeds the incumbent's.
  - REUSE-GATED: same, but accept only if the gain exceeds
    3 * sqrt(p(1-p)/n), p = incumbent score.
- n in {500, 1000, 4000, 16000}. 20 seeds per cell.
- gap = reported score on the reused set minus population accuracy.

## Predictions

- P1. REUSE-NAIVE gap at generation 100, n = 4000, lies in [0.08, 0.25].
- P2. REUSE-NAIVE gap at generation 100 scales as n^(-1/2): log-log slope
  across the four n values lies in [-0.6, -0.4].
- P3. Phantom share of reported gain over generations 51-100,
  1 - (true gain)/(reported gain), exceeds 0.5 in REUSE-NAIVE for
  n in {500, 1000, 4000}.
- P4a. At n = 4000, REUSE-GATED gap at generation 100 is at most half the
  REUSE-NAIVE gap.
- P4b. At n = 4000, final population accuracy orders
  FRESH > REUSE-NAIVE > REUSE-GATED.
- P5. At n = 4000 in REUSE-NAIVE, the late/early gain ratio
  (gain over 51-100)/(gain over 1-50) computed from reported scores is at
  least twice the same ratio computed from population accuracy.

## Not modeled

- Item-level feedback (the loop seeing which items failed). Score-only here.
- Stochastic evaluation noise. Evaluation is deterministic.
- Any real model. This is a property of the toy and its parameters.

# Eval-reuse toy runs (2026-10-11)

Seeded simulations behind the "synthetic mechanism result" rows of
`paper/evaluation_feedback_insertions.md`. They are JavaScript, not exact, and
involve no language model. Files are stored as run; `output/**` is not
line-normalized, so the recorded hashes remain checkable.

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `PREREG.md`, `sim.js`, `SEAL.txt`, `results.json` | Run 1: parametric model, score-only reuse. Predictions and script hashed before execution. |
| `PREREG_2.md`, `sim2.js`, `SEAL_2.txt`, `results2.json` | Run 2: 3-nearest-neighbour learner, item-level feedback. Predictions and script hashed before execution. |
| `sim2b.js`, `results2b.json` | Post hoc arm added after run 2's results were seen. Exploratory. Hashes appended to `SEAL_2.txt` afterwards. |

`results.json` from run 1 was not hashed at the time. Its hash, recorded when
these files were copied here, is `9149c1083716e4f901d0d728ede77a90abf8b9385a9ecf207e5bb47bc8f8a8bd`. That is a receipt for the copy, not a
seal on the run.

Reproduce with plain Node, from a scratch copy so existing results are kept:

```powershell
node sim.js
node sim2.js
node sim2b.js
```

Each script overwrites its results file in its own directory.

Prediction record: 5 of 6 passed in run 1, 3 of 6 in run 2. Both runs
overpredicted the size of the gap between reported and true accuracy.

A re-run from a scratch copy on the same day, in the environment that produced
them, reproduced all three results files byte for byte.

A second re-run on Node 24.19.0 under Windows reproduced `results2.json` and
`results2b.json` byte for byte. `results.json` differed in the last digit of 24
floating-point values, the largest relative difference about 1.2e-15. Its
`summary` and `checks` were identical. Run 1 is reproducible to its reported
precision, not to the byte, across platforms.
